titre: The 1851 Crystal Palace Was Designed by a Gardener
accroche: The Great Exhibition committee rejects 245 designs. The one it chooses comes from a gardener who said he drew inspiration from water lily leaves.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1850, London is preparing the Great Exhibition and looking for a building that can house, under one roof, the machines, textiles and sculptures of the whole world. The building committee issues a call for designs, open to foreigners too: in three weeks it receives some 245 proposals, 38 of them from abroad, and rejects them all. In the end, the design it finally chooses is that of Joseph Paxton, head gardener to the Duke of Devonshire at Chatsworth.

## A greenhouse on the scale of a palace

Paxton runs the gardens at Chatsworth. He has built glass greenhouses there, including a great conservatory begun in 1836 and completed in 1840. In 1849, he succeeds in making the Victoria regia, now Victoria amazonica, a giant water lily, bloom for the first time in Europe: a seedling was entrusted to him that year, and two months later its leaves already measured 1.4 meters across. He has a larger greenhouse built for it, and would later say that its great ribbed leaves, floating on the water, were a major inspiration for his design.

On June 11, 1850, at a meeting of the board of directors of the Midland Railway in Derby, Paxton sketches his plan on a sheet of pink blotting paper, now held at the Victoria and Albert Museum. His horticultural staff turn it into proper drawings, for time is short: plans, calculations and estimates are ready in under two weeks. The commission endorses his design in July 1850, less than a year before the opening. The building is made of iron and glass, from prefabricated parts: some sections go up eighteen hours after leaving the factory, and the whole is ready to receive exhibitors in only five months. It opens to the public in Hyde Park on May 1, 1851. Knighted in 1851, when the building was completed, Paxton then sees it dismantled, rebuilt, modified and enlarged at Sydenham, in south London, where it reopens in June 1854.

## What it changes

The design that beats out 245 others is that of a gardener, who had already built greenhouses at Chatsworth. The Dictionary of National Biography notes that his great conservatory at Chatsworth formed, in some respects, the model for the 1851 building, and the water lily house is given as the direct origin of his design. From water lily to palace, the line of descent runs through the greenhouse.

repere.texte: The design of Joseph Paxton, head gardener at Chatsworth, sketched on June 11, 1850 on pink blotting paper during a meeting of the board of directors of the Midland Railway in Derby, is chosen by the commissioners of the Great Exhibition, in part because the designs of all the other architects had been rejected.
repere.source: Victoria and Albert Museum, online collections

carte.punch: The 1851 Crystal Palace was designed by a gardener.
carte.idee: In 1850, the committee of London's Great Exhibition rejects all 245 designs it received. The commission endorses the one by Joseph Paxton, the Duke of Devonshire's gardener, an iron-and-glass structure for which he cited the ribbed leaves of a giant water lily as a major inspiration.

quiz.question: What inspiration did Joseph Paxton, a gardener, cite for the structure of the Crystal Palace?
choix: The great ribbed leaves of a giant water lily, which he had made bloom in a greenhouse at Chatsworth
The plans of an architect on the building committee, who signed the design under his own name
The plan of a stone palace drawn by one of the competition's architects, which he supposedly just enlarged
Gothic cathedrals, whose flying buttresses he reproduced in iron and glass
quiz.explication: Paxton cited the great ribbed leaves of the Victoria regia, which he had made bloom at Chatsworth, as a major inspiration. The design is a sketch in his own hand (V&A), endorsed by the commission; the building is made of prefabricated iron and glass, not stone. None of the sources consulted reports that he cited Gothic cathedrals.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many designs did the Great Exhibition's building committee receive before choosing Paxton's?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In three weeks, the committee receives some 245 designs and rejects them all, before endorsing Paxton's in July 1850.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where and how did Joseph Paxton first sketch the Crystal Palace design?
choix: On direct commission from the Duke of Devonshire, who had supplied him with a brief
On a sheet of blotting paper, during a railway board meeting
On the plans of an existing greenhouse at Chatsworth, which he simply enlarged
On a wall of his office, with the help of an architect hired for the occasion
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On June 11, 1850, at a meeting of the board of directors of the Midland Railway in Derby, Paxton sketches his plan on a sheet of pink blotting paper.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What became of the Crystal Palace after the Great Exhibition ended in Hyde Park?
choix: It was sold to an American industrialist who had it shipped to New York
It was destroyed by fire a few months after closing
It was left standing in Hyde Park and turned into a permanent museum
It was dismantled, then rebuilt on a larger scale at Sydenham in 1854
quiz_supplementaire.explication: After the Exhibition, the building is rebuilt, modified and enlarged at Sydenham, in south London, where it reopens in June 1854.
